Hill-function nonlinearity in state transitions creates bistable \\\"affordance landscapes\\\" that gate behavioural mode switching. Crucially, replacing Hill-function dynamics with linear transitions reduces the chaotic-itinerancy detection rate from 80% to 20%, demonstrating that nonlinear affordance structure is necessary for generating metastable switching. We further show that agents with simplified internal models of the world sustain richer itinerant dynamics as a group than \\\"perfect-foresight\\\" agents, suggesting that bounded rationality may be functionally advantageous for maintaining behavioural flexibility.
